paragraphs: Large language models create hardware challenges because their billions of parameters require substantial memory and computation. Quantization addresses this by representing values with fewer bits. The paper focuses on a tension in existing low-bit approaches: some struggle with unusually large or otherwise atypical values, while others sacrifice hardware efficiency to represent the data more accurately.

The authors propose Bi-Exponent Block Floating Point, or BiE, together with a new quantization procedure. Their central idea is that the numerical format itself has room for improvement. A small bit budget does not uniquely determine which values can be represented well; changing the representation can make it better suited to the unusual distributions found in language models.

Across the models and benchmarks examined, the authors report better accuracy and favorable hardware characteristics. The contribution therefore concerns both numerical representation and its practical use in quantization. The findings suggest that choosing a more expressive low-bit format can help address the accuracy and efficiency trade-off, rather than treating that trade-off solely as a matter of how aggressively values are compressed.
icml-2024-bie-bi-exponent-block-floating.tldr: BiE introduces a low-bit numerical format and quantization procedure that improve reported accuracy while remaining hardware-friendly.

paragraphs: COALA is a platform and benchmark suite for studying federated learning under a wider range of computer vision conditions. Its organizing idea is that practical challenges arise at three distinct levels: what clients are learning, what data they have, and what models they use. This makes the platform a way to examine several sources of variation within one framework.

At the task level, COALA supports 15 vision tasks, including detection, segmentation, and pose estimation, as well as clients learning multiple tasks simultaneously. At the data level, it includes supervised, semi-supervised, and unsupervised settings. It also considers differences in input features, beyond differences in class frequencies, and continual learning when data changes over time.

At the model level, the benchmarks cover split models and clients using different models. Users can customize configurations, individual components, or entire workflows. The authors systematically benchmark these scenarios and identify opportunities for improvement. The main contribution is broader experimental infrastructure: it makes federated learning research address combinations of tasks, data conditions, and model arrangements that simpler classification settings leave unexplored.
icml-2024-coala-a-practical-and-vision-c.tldr: COALA broadens federated learning evaluation with customizable benchmarks spanning vision tasks, changing data conditions, and heterogeneous models.

paragraphs: Few-shot class-incremental learning asks a model to keep learning new categories from only a handful of examples after initially training on well-represented categories. This paper approaches the problem through composition: previously learned visual primitives can be reused and combined to describe new categories. The motivation comes from accounts of how people assemble new concepts from familiar components.

The proposed model compares sets of primitives and contains two complementary modules. The composition module uses Centered Kernel Alignment to approximate similarity between primitive sets, allowing training and evaluation to operate on combinations of components. The reuse module classifies inputs after replacing primitives with the closest primitives from other classes, encouraging components to remain useful across category boundaries.

Experiments on three datasets show improvements over the state-of-the-art methods considered, along with improved interpretability. The approach matters because it gives learning from scarce examples an explicit structure: new categories can draw on reusable visual knowledge instead of depending entirely on their own limited samples. Its interpretation of categories as compositions also provides a clearer account of how previously learned information contributes to new recognition decisions.
icml-2024-compositional-few-shot-class-i.tldr: A compositional model reuses visual primitives to learn new classes from few examples, improving reported accuracy and interpretability.

paragraphs: Homomorphic encryption offers a way to run model computations while separating what the model owner and data owner know. Applying it to transformers has been difficult because the models must be converted into a compatible polynomial form. This paper addresses that architectural and mathematical obstacle, extending an approach previously studied mainly with convolutional neural networks.

The authors introduce a transformer architecture tailored to homomorphic encryption and a method for converting its operators into polynomial equivalents. They present this as the first polynomial transformer and the first demonstration of secure inference with complete transformers under homomorphic encryption. Their evaluation includes both language models and vision transformers across several datasets and tasks.

The resulting models achieve performance comparable to traditional transformers of similar scale. The authors also examine stability and use ablations to assess how individual components contribute. These findings support the viability of converting whole transformer models into an encrypted-inference-compatible form while retaining useful task performance. The contribution combines an executable architecture with a conversion method, addressing the model as a complete computational system.
icml-2024-converting-transformers-to-pol.tldr: A polynomial transformer architecture enables secure homomorphic-encryption inference with reported performance comparable to similarly sized conventional transformers.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a pretrained vision-language model can weaken the broad knowledge that helps it handle unfamiliar inputs. CRoFT addresses two kinds of unfamiliarity together: changes in how known classes look, such as a different image style, and the appearance of entirely unseen classes. The desired behavior is to recognize familiar categories despite visual changes while detecting inputs from new categories.

The paper introduces an out-of-distribution detection objective that also supports generalization. Its central result connects reducing the gradient magnitude of energy scores on training data with making the curvature of the classification loss consistent across domains. The theoretical analysis identifies this consistency, expressed through Hessians, as a strong indicator of generalization under distribution shift.

This connection motivates a unified fine-tuning framework that optimizes detection and generalization concurrently. The authors report superior experimental performance for their method. The significance is that the two goals share a training mechanism: an objective designed to help identify unfamiliar classes can also encourage properties associated with recognizing known classes under changed conditions. The theoretical connection supports that design without making generalization an unconditional guarantee.
icml-2024-croft-robust-fine-tuning-with-.tldr: CRoFT jointly improves robustness to changed visual conditions and detection of unseen classes through a shared fine-tuning objective.

paragraphs: In-context reinforcement learning studies whether transformers can adapt to tasks and environments through the histories provided in their context. Existing approaches impose demanding data requirements: histories may need to come from reinforcement learning agents, or actions must be labeled by an optimal policy. This paper investigates whether a different data acquisition process can relax those requirements.

The proposed approach, ADε, constructs a curriculum through synthetic noise injection. The authors show that such a curriculum can produce learning histories suitable for in-context reinforcement learning. The key change is in how the training experience is assembled: noise supplies a means of constructing the curriculum without relying on the same optimal-policy data requirements.

Experiments demonstrate that the need for generation using optimal policies can be reduced. The resulting in-context learner outperforms the best suboptimal policy in its learning dataset by a reported factor of two. This finding is significant because the learned behavior can exceed the strongest suboptimal policy supplying the data. It supports noise-based curricula as a viable route to acquiring useful learning histories under the studied conditions.
icml-2024-emergence-of-in-context-reinfo.tldr: ADε uses synthetic noise curricula to enable in-context reinforcement learning while reducing reliance on optimal-policy training data.

paragraphs: This paper studies a simple robustness question in multiple-choice answering: does changing the order of answer options change a model's behavior? Reordering an answer set preserves the available choices, so a reliable answer should ideally depend on their content rather than their position. The authors investigate this issue in both language models and vision-language models.

Their experiments show that adversarial permutations of answer options can exploit a vulnerability in popular models. The problem appears across different model sizes and also in models described in the study as very recent. This breadth matters because the observed sensitivity is not confined to a single model size or to systems that process only text.

The finding identifies an accessible way to probe whether apparent answering ability remains stable under a small presentation change. A model may handle the underlying question successfully while still being vulnerable to a particular ordering of the same choices. The paper therefore contributes evidence about permutation sensitivity as a specific obstacle to trustworthy multiple-choice use, with code supplied to reproduce its experiments.
icml-2024-fool-your-vision-and-language-.tldr: Experiments show that simply reordering multiple-choice answers can exploit vulnerabilities in language and vision-language models across sizes.

paragraphs: GPTSwarm represents language-model agents as computational graphs, providing a common structure for approaches that otherwise live in separate prompt-engineering codebases. Each node performs an operation, such as processing multimodal data or querying a language model. Edges specify how information moves between those operations, making an agent's workflow an explicit object that can be manipulated.

Individual graphs can be combined recursively into larger graphs representing collaboration among agents. Connections can then link operations belonging to different agents. The framework introduces two forms of automatic optimization: changing the prompts used at individual nodes and changing graph connections to improve how agents coordinate. These address both local instructions and the broader organization of computation.

Experiments demonstrate that this representation supports efficient development, integration, and automatic improvement of different language agents. The approach matters because prompt quality and collaboration structure become parts of the same optimizable system. Developers can express an agent, compose it with others, and improve the resulting workflow within a shared abstraction rather than rebuilding each arrangement as a separate implementation.
icml-2024-gptswarm-language-agents-as-op.tldr: GPTSwarm models language agents as composable graphs and automatically improves both their prompts and their information flow.

paragraphs: Hybrid models combine mechanistic differential equations with flexible neural networks. The equations bring scientific structure and causal grounding, while the neural components increase expressive power. This paper addresses a tension in that combination: as the learned components become more flexible, the causal grounding supplied by the mechanistic model can be lost, even though prediction remains a central training goal.

The authors add another kind of domain knowledge: rankings of treatment effects across interventions. Such rankings can be available even when the exact size of each effect is unknown. They encode this information in a causal loss and combine it with the usual predictive loss. The combined objective biases training toward hybrid models that respect the supplied causal relationships.

The method is evaluated on glucose dynamics following exercise in people with type 1 diabetes. The authors report state-of-the-art predictive performance together with causal validity in this application. The contribution shows how partial intervention knowledge can guide a flexible scientific model: knowing which effects should be larger can help preserve causal behavior without requiring precise treatment-effect values.
icml-2024-hybrid-2-neural-ode-causal-mod.tldr: A loss based on treatment-effect rankings helps hybrid neural ODE models combine strong glucose predictions with causal validity.

paragraphs: Theory of Mind involves reasoning about mental states, including what different people believe. Language models display some abilities on tasks requiring this kind of reasoning, but their internal mechanisms are less clear. This paper investigates whether information about different agents' beliefs is represented inside the models, rather than examining task answers alone.

The researchers find that belief status from several agents' perspectives can be recovered from neural activations using a linear decoder. This indicates that the activations contain accessible information distinguishing those perspectives. They then manipulate the identified representations and observe large changes in Theory of Mind performance, connecting the internal information to the models' behavior on these tasks.

The findings also extend to varied social reasoning tasks involving different patterns of causal inference. That result suggests the representations may have usefulness beyond a single task format. The evidence combines decoding with intervention: one establishes that belief-related information is present, while the other shows that changing it affects performance. Together, these observations support a functional role for the representations in the social reasoning studied.
icml-2024-language-models-represent-beli.tldr: Language-model activations encode agents' belief states, and manipulating those representations substantially changes social reasoning performance.

paragraphs: Evidence linking the hippocampus to both spatial navigation and language comprehension motivates this paper's search for a shared computational mechanism. The authors build PHE-trinity, a model inspired by the prefrontal, hippocampal, and entorhinal systems. Its purpose is to investigate whether mechanisms associated with spatial representation can also support the structured processing needed for language commands.

The model has two central features. A modular continuous attractor neural network represents syntactic structure, drawing an analogy with entorhinal grid networks. Two separate input streams reflect the separation of structure and content described in the hippocampal formation. Together, these choices make the relationship between language structure and the network's dynamics part of the model's design.

Evaluations on the SCAN command-parsing dataset show that attractor dynamics can support systematic generalization and learning from limited data. Visualization and reverse engineering also reveal a possible dynamic mechanism through which a grid network could represent syntax. The work provides an initial computational account of a potential connection between navigation and language processing, with the biological interpretation presented as a possibility supported by the model.
icml-2024-leveraging-attractor-dynamics-.tldr: PHE-trinity uses navigation-inspired attractor dynamics to support language parsing, systematic generalization, and learning from limited data.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning can be treated as sequence prediction using recorded experience and information such as eventual rewards or goals. The paper argues that this supervised formulation can neglect the central reinforcement learning objective of maximizing return. That omission limits trajectory stitching: the ability to combine useful portions of recorded trajectories when the available behavior is suboptimal.

Reinformer adds return maximization directly to sequence-model training. It aims to predict the highest future return within the data distribution, then uses that predicted return to guide action selection at inference time. The distinction is consequential: the model is trained to identify a high-return target supported by its distribution, as well as to model sequences conditioned on outcomes.

On the D4RL benchmark, Reinformer is competitive with classical reinforcement learning methods and outperforms the state-of-the-art sequence model considered, particularly in trajectory stitching. These results support integrating the optimization objective into sequence learning when recorded trajectories are imperfect. The predicted maximum remains explicitly tied to the distribution, which defines the kind of return the method aims to pursue.
icml-2024-reinformer-max-return-sequence.tldr: Reinformer trains sequence models to maximize in-distribution future returns, improving their ability to stitch together useful recorded behavior.

paragraphs: Vision-language instruction tuning can introduce safety problems even when the underlying language model has already been aligned. The authors' initial analysis attributes harmful behavior to harmful examples in the training data and finds that this tuning can cause previously learned safety behavior to be forgotten. The paper addresses this problem through targeted training data.

The authors curate VLGuard, a vision-language instruction-following dataset covering multiple harmful categories. They test two ways of using it: incorporating it into standard vision-language fine-tuning and applying it in an additional fine-tuning stage afterward. Both routes allow the same resource to support safety alignment at different points in model development.

Experiments show effective rejection of unsafe instructions and substantial reductions in the success of several black-box attacks, with success rates approaching zero in many tested cases. These improvements have minimal negative impact on helpfulness and sometimes improve it. The findings support safety-focused data as a practical way to strengthen the evaluated models, while the dataset also serves as a resource for testing existing models and training or safeguarding others.
icml-2024-safety-fine-tuning-at-almost-n.tldr: VLGuard safety fine-tuning reduces harmful responses and attack success in vision-language models with little or no loss of helpfulness.

paragraphs: Learning theory often studies independent observations, but this paper considers dependent data and squared prediction loss. Existing finite-sample bounds commonly penalize the variance term through the mixing time, which measures how dependence persists. Such penalties can make a dataset behave, in the bound, as though it contained substantially fewer useful observations.

The authors study hypothesis classes with controlled tail behavior in an Orlicz space. When the L2 and Orlicz topologies are comparable on the class, they show that empirical risk minimization achieves a leading error term governed by class complexity and second-order statistics. Direct dependence on mixing moves into an additive higher-order term instead of multiplying the leading term.

Their proof uses mixed-tail generic chaining and yields sharp, instance-optimal rates within the framework. Applicable examples include sub-Gaussian linear regression and bounded smoothness classes. The result is described as nearly mixing-free because mixing still appears in the bound, but its direct role is restricted. The comparability assumption is central to obtaining this more precise account of learning from dependent observations.
icml-2024-sharp-rates-in-dependent-learn.tldr: Under a comparability condition on the hypothesis class, squared-loss learning bounds avoid a direct mixing penalty in their leading term.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning policies can embody expensive simulation, expertise, and real-world validation. This paper examines whether their behavior can be copied through black-box access under unusually restricted conditions. Stealthy Imitation is presented as the first policy-stealing attack that requires neither access to the environment nor knowledge of the input range.

Without access to the states normally encountered by the target policy, the method fits a reward model to approximate the missing input-state distribution. The authors also report a counterintuitive finding: the victim becomes harder to imitate when the attack-query distribution matches the victim's distribution. This makes the relationship between query selection and successful imitation an important part of the study.

Across diverse high-dimensional control tasks, Stealthy Imitation consistently outperforms earlier data-free approaches adapted to policy stealing. The paper also proposes a countermeasure that substantially reduces the attack's effectiveness. Together, the results identify a policy-copying threat under limited attacker knowledge and demonstrate that its success can be meaningfully reduced by a defense in the evaluated setting.
icml-2024-stealthy-imitation-reward-guid.tldr: Stealthy Imitation copies control policies without environment access or known input ranges, while a proposed defense substantially reduces its effectiveness.

paragraphs: Neural-network architectures commonly create symmetries in their loss functions. This paper studies how those symmetries shape learning behavior and the structure of learned parameters. Its central claim is that symmetry can do more than describe equivalent model configurations: under particular training conditions, it can lead the model toward a constrained solution.

The authors prove that each mirror-reflection symmetry with reflection surface O induces a parameter constraint expressed as O-transpose times theta equals zero. The constrained solution is reached when either weight decay or gradient noise is large. They derive structural consequences for common symmetries: rescaling leads to sparsity, rotation to low rank, and permutation to homogeneous ensembling.

The framework is then used to explain loss of plasticity and several collapse phenomena in neural networks. It also suggests an algorithmic use for symmetry: enforcing hard constraints through a differentiable procedure. The result ties architectural symmetry, training conditions, and parameter structure into one account. Its conditional nature matters, because the stated emergence of the constrained solution depends on sufficiently large weight decay or gradient noise.
icml-2024-symmetry-induces-structure-and.tldr: The paper shows how loss symmetries induce parameter constraints under large weight decay or gradient noise, explaining several learned structures and collapse phenomena.

paragraphs: Spiking transformers combine strong task performance with the energy advantages of spiking computation, yet training them on GPUs can take substantially longer than training conventional neural-network counterparts. This paper investigates token sparsification as a way to reduce that burden. The authors find that conventional sparsification methods cause noticeable performance losses in this setting.

They propose STATA, which combines timestep-wise anchor tokens with two attention-alignment mechanisms. The anchor tokens provide standardized criteria for identifying important tokens across timesteps. The intra- and inter-alignment components operate on attention maps to improve weaker attention. Together, these mechanisms address both which tokens are retained and how attention is learned during sparsification.

Experiments across multiple datasets and architectures report training speedups of up to approximately 1.53 times and energy reductions of approximately 48%, with comparable task performance. These results show that token sparsification can deliver useful efficiency gains when adapted to the temporal structure of spiking transformers. The reported improvements support the framework as a way to reduce training costs while maintaining performance in the evaluated configurations.
icml-2024-towards-efficient-spiking-tran.tldr: STATA adapts token sparsification to spiking transformers, reporting up to roughly 1.53× faster training and roughly 48% lower energy use with comparable performance.

paragraphs: Transformers can underperform specialized architectures on tasks requiring long-range dependencies. This paper investigates what attention can learn from long-range layers, including state-space models, linear recurrent layers, and global convolutions. Its central question is whether small architectural changes can recover some of their advantages without introducing a substantially larger or more expensive model.

The authors identify smoothness and locality as two key principles for these tasks. They incorporate biases toward both into the attention mechanism. These modifications add no trainable parameters and require only negligible additional computation, making the changes a way to alter how the architecture approaches the task without increasing its learned parameter count.

On the Long Range Arena benchmark, the modified transformers improve substantially and narrow the gap with specialized long-range layers. Theory and experiments also examine why conventional transformers perform less well in this setting. The findings support the importance of architectural biases for capturing long-range relationships: useful changes can come from how attention is organized, even when the number of trainable parameters stays the same.
icml-2024-viewing-transformers-through-t.tldr: Adding smoothness and locality biases to attention improves long-range benchmark performance without adding trainable parameters.

paragraphs: Multimodal variational autoencoders must combine information from individual modalities to estimate joint distributions and evaluate their training objective. The paper argues that common product- and mixture-of-experts approaches make an overly optimistic independence assumption when aggregating those distributions. It proposes a way to account for dependence when deciding how different sources of information should contribute.

The method uses consensus of dependent experts, abbreviated CoDE. It introduces a new evidence lower bound that approximates the joint likelihood by learning the contribution of each subset of modalities. This makes combinations of modalities part of the aggregation process, providing a mechanism for incorporating relationships that an independence-based treatment overlooks.

The resulting CoDE-VAE achieves a better balance between generative coherence and quality, alongside more precise log-likelihood estimates. It also reduces the generative quality gap as modality count increases and, in some cases, reaches quality similar to unimodal VAEs. Classification accuracy remains comparable to state-of-the-art multimodal VAE models. The findings suggest that explicitly accommodating dependence can improve generation and likelihood estimation while retaining competitive classification performance.
icml-2025-aggregation-of-dependent-exper.tldr: CoDE-VAE accounts for dependence between modalities, improving reported generation trade-offs and likelihood estimates while retaining competitive classification accuracy.

paragraphs: Graph cut sparsification seeks a graph representation that preserves the values of cuts, which divide vertices into two groups. This paper studies the problem under differential privacy. Previous efficient private methods had additive error scaling roughly as n to the power 1.5, while exponentially expensive methods could achieve roughly linear additive error, alongside a multiplicative approximation.

The authors give a polynomial-time algorithm for non-negatively weighted graphs that produces a differentially private synthetic graph. It approximates every cut with multiplicative error 1 + gamma and additive error n to the power 1.25 + o(1), setting aside dependencies on the privacy parameters and gamma. The improved exponent breaks the stated additive-error barrier for efficient private algorithms.

The technical centerpiece is a private algorithm for expander decomposition, adapting a powerful graph-algorithm technique to the privacy setting. The result matters because it improves the accuracy available with polynomial-time computation, moving toward the stronger guarantees previously associated with inefficient methods. Both additive and multiplicative errors remain part of the guarantee, and the improvement concerns the stated dependence on graph size.
icml-2025-breaking-the-n-1-5-additive-er.tldr: A private expander-decomposition method enables polynomial-time graph cut approximation with additive error n^(1.25 + o(1)), improving the previous n^1.5 barrier.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can struggle when asked to handle unseen or out-of-distribution data, particularly when their training examples are limited or insufficiently diverse. This paper studies data augmentation as a response to that problem. Its approach connects a theoretical analysis of generalization with the design of an efficient augmentation algorithm.

The theoretical framework uses Rademacher complexity to derive a regret bound on generalization error and characterize how augmentation affects it. This analysis informs GRATIN, an augmentation method based on Gaussian mixture models. The method draws on the ability of Gaussian mixtures to approximate distributions, making distribution modeling central to how additional graph data is constructed.

The authors report better generalization than existing augmentation techniques together with improved time complexity. These findings make the contribution twofold: the framework supplies a way to reason about augmentation's effect, and GRATIN turns that reasoning into a practical method. The result supports distribution-based augmentation as a promising means of improving graph learning when the original data offers limited size or diversity.
icml-2025-graph-neural-network-generaliz.tldr: GRATIN uses Gaussian mixture models and generalization theory to improve graph data augmentation, with reported gains in generalization and time complexity.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how predictions can improve approximation algorithms for difficult graph problems. The predictions may come from past data and provide partial information about an optimal solution. The authors extend an existing prediction framework to an edge-based setting, where each edge supplies two bits predicting whether its two endpoints belong to an optimal solution.

Even when each bit is only weakly correlated with the true solution, the authors show that this additional information can overcome approximation barriers from the standard setting. They develop improved approximation ratios for problems including MaxCut, Vertex Cover, Set Cover, and Maximum Independent Set. The result depends on the stated prediction model, which supplies information unavailable to ordinary algorithms.

A common strategy runs through the algorithms: use predictions to satisfy constraints associated with high-degree vertices, handle low-degree vertices without predictions, and carefully combine the two answers. This division explains how weak predictive information can still be useful. It concentrates that information on one part of the problem while retaining conventional algorithmic reasoning for the rest.
icml-2025-improved-approximations-for-ha.tldr: Weak edge-based predictions enable improved approximation algorithms by guiding high-degree constraints while conventional methods handle low-degree vertices.

paragraphs: The paper studies private estimation of a single quantile, such as the median, from distributed data. Each user holds one value in a domain of size B and can be queried once through a private mechanism. The central question is whether adaptively choosing queries can reduce how many users are needed compared with fixing the queries in advance.

The authors propose one protocol under local differential privacy and another under shuffle differential privacy. For target error alpha, the local protocol requires O(log B divided by epsilon squared alpha squared) users. The shuffle protocol requires approximately (1/epsilon squared + 1/alpha squared) log B users, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Both improve on prior nonadaptive requirements by several logarithmic factors in B.

Matching lower bounds establish optimality of the local protocol in the low-epsilon regime. Additional lower bounds for nonadaptive protocols prove a fundamental separation between adaptive and nonadaptive approaches. The contribution therefore goes beyond proposing lighter protocols: it identifies a setting where adapting queries provides a provable statistical advantage, even though each participant is contacted only once.
icml-2025-lightweight-protocols-for-dist.tldr: Adaptive private quantile protocols reduce user requirements and establish a provable advantage over nonadaptive approaches.

paragraphs: Fluent text generation does not by itself produce an agent that pursues goals across multiple interactions. The paper highlights behaviors such as asking clarifying questions, gathering information, and choosing actions that improve later decisions. Reinforcement learning offers a route toward such behavior, but developing reliable methods requires accessible tasks that evaluate progress over multiple turns.

LMRL Gym provides a benchmark and an open-source research framework for that purpose. The benchmark contains eight tasks: three interactive dialogue tasks and five reinforcement learning capability tests. These span open-ended dialogue and text games, requiring repeated language interaction and covering different properties relevant to training goal-directed agents.

The accompanying framework supports offline value-based and online policy-based reinforcement learning methods. This gives researchers infrastructure for beginning experiments as well as shared evaluation tasks. The contribution is a foundation for studying intentional, temporally extended language behavior. It makes multi-turn decision-making the object of evaluation, so algorithm development can address how an interaction unfolds and whether earlier actions help achieve later goals.
icml-2025-lmrl-gym-benchmarks-for-multi-.tldr: LMRL Gym supplies eight multi-turn language tasks and a research framework for developing and evaluating reinforcement-learning-based language agents.

paragraphs: This paper asks when training on a small number of tasks can support a much larger family of unseen tasks. It studies an autoregressive compositional setting: each task consists of T operations, and each operation comes from a collection of D subtasks. Combining those choices produces D to the power T possible tasks.

The authors show theoretically that generalization across this entire family is achievable with training on only roughly D tasks, up to logarithmic factors. The compositional structure is central to the result: a relatively small collection of reusable operations can give rise to exponentially many combinations. The claim concerns what is achievable in this structured setting.

Experiments demonstrate this form of exponential task generalization in transformers on sparse parity functions using in-context learning and chain-of-thought reasoning. Further demonstrations cover arithmetic and language translation. Together, the theory and experiments support composition as an explanation for how limited task exposure can lead to broad generalization. Learning reusable operations and applying them in new sequences can substantially expand the range of tasks a model handles.
icml-2025-task-generalization-with-autor.tldr: Under autoregressive compositional structure, training on roughly D tasks can theoretically support D^T tasks, with transformer experiments demonstrating exponential generalization.
